       1             Thank you for coming out this morning for

       1             I do have an opening statement, if we're

       2      going to proceed to stay in this room.

       3             SENATOR O'MARA:  Okay.

       4             SENATOR TKACZYK:  First of all, I want to

       5      thank you for holding this hearing.  The timing is

       6      impeccable.

       7             I think there's near unanimous agreement that

       8      our political system is broken, and needs fixing.

       9             The Governor, the Assembly Democratic

      10      Conference, The Senate Democratic Conference, and

      11      the Senate's Independent Democratic Conference, all

      12      acknowledge that our current finance system is

      13      outdated, too lax, and in desperate need of reform.

      14             And poll after poll shows that an

      15      overwhelming majority of New Yorkers believe we must

      16      reduce the influence of money in politics.

      17             Just today, I got a bipartisan survey that

      18      said:  7 in 10 likely voters believe campaign

      19      finance reform would be effective at reducing the

      20      influence of money in politics.  And the same

      21      percentage believe reform needs to -- would help end

      22      corruption in state government.

      23             But it appears that the Senate Republicans

      24      seem to be advocating to maintain the status quo, in

      25      which corporate money and special interests outweigh





 

                                                                   9
       1      the will of the people.

       2             Clearly, the status quo is no longer

       3      sufficient.

       4             We need -- we can no longer ignore the

       5      problems and corruption plaguing our current

       6      campaign finance system, so let's use this hearing

       7      as a starting point for real reform.

       8             Last month, I suggested that the

       9      Elections Committee hold public hearings over some

      10      large issues concerning our campaign finance system.

      11             Questions I was hoping to address in those

      12      hearings included:

      13             What can the Legislature do to make elections

      14      more fair, and how can we remove the influence of

      15      big money and dark money from our government and the

      16      electoral process?

      17             What can be done to ensure that more eligible

      18      voters take the time to cast their ballot, and how

      19      can we protect the voting rights of those voters?

      20             While this hearing is not as broad as I had

      21      hoped, it is a start.

      22             And, I welcome the opportunity to gain

      23      insight into how we can make our electoral process

      24      more open, more fair, and transparent to public

      25      scrutiny.





 

                                                                   10
       1             I'm pleased that there are advocates from

       2      both sides of the issue testifying today, but I'm

       3      dismayed that -- as I mentioned earlier, that we do

       4      not have organizations here that would like to

       5      participate.

       6             I find it ironic that, in this discussion in

       7      which first amendment rights are an overarching

       8      theme, we are barring many experts and interested

       9      parties from offering their opinions on how we can

      10      make our system more open, transparent, fair, and

      11      free from the influence of big money and special

      12      interests.

      13             I do look forward to hearing from the experts

      14      who are going to be here today.

      15             I hope, at the very least, we can all agree,

      16      and acknowledge, that our current campaign finance

      17      regulatory system is broken -- broken, and ignoring

      18      its problems and maintaining status quo is no longer

      19      acceptable.

      20             It's time to strengthen the laws, increase

      21      disclosure requirements, increase transparency, and

      22      increase accountability among our elected officials.

      23             We also need to level the playing field on

      24      how we elect people to office, by ensuring that our

      25      campaign finance reform includes supporting small





 

                                                                   11
       1      donations.

       2             And, lastly, we must increase our enforcement

       3      efforts to punish those who do not comply with the

       4      law.

       5             I would like to thank you, Chairman O'Mara,

       6      and I look forward to working with you,

       7      Governor Cuomo, and our legislative leaders on

       8      reforming the state's campaign finance regulations,

       9      and restoring New Yorkers' faith in their state

      10      government.

      11             Thank you.

      12             SENATOR O'MARA:  Thank you, Senator.

      13             Any other senator wish to make any remarks?

      14             Then we will commence with David Keating.

      15             Good morning.

      16             DAVID KEATING:  Good morning.

      17             Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

      18             SENATOR O'MARA:  I just want to lay the

      19      ground rules a little bit here.

      20             We're going to try to keep the testimony to

      21      approximately ten minutes, if that's possible, and

      22      then leave time for questions, so that we can move

      23      through the list of witnesses that we have here

      24      today.

      25             DAVID KEATING:  Great.





 

                                                                   12
       1             Well, I'll try to stay within that time

       2      frame.

       3             Thank you very much for the opportunity to

       4      speak before you today.

       5             I grew up in Long Island, I went to college

       6      in New York as well, so it's great to be back in the

       7      Empire State.

       8             I represent a group known as the Center for

       9      Competitive Politics, which is a non-partisan,

      10      non-profit group focused on promoting and protecting

      11      first amendment political rights of speech,

      12      assembly, and petition.

      13             And, if you do want to look for models to

      14      emulate, I would not urge you to emulate

      15      New York City's model, or other states with

      16      so-called "strict campaign finance regimes."

      17             There's no evidence that any of this works,

      18      there's no evidence that it reduces corruption, and

      19      there's no evidence that it increases the

      20      competitiveness of elections.

      21             If you want to look at a model state, I would

      22      say, look to Oregon.

      23             A lot of the members of this Legislature

      24      probably have a great affinity for Oregon.  It's

      25      seen as a progressive state, very innovative.  And





 

                                                                   13
       1      it has probably the most liberated liberal campaign

       2      finance laws in the country; and, yet, year after

       3      year, it produces state government officials that

       4      are highly respected.  Seen as not -- very low rates

       5      of corruption.

       6             It's basically a model.

       7             So if you want to look at a model, I would

       8      encourage you to look at Oregon, and try to adopt

       9      Oregon's model, not New York City's model.

      10             Now, proponents of clean elections like to

      11      tout these programs as a panacea for eliminating

      12      corruption and fixing government.

      13             But if you look at the states that have

      14      adopted these proposals, there's no evidence that

      15      any of this works.

      16             The rates of corruption are not lower with

      17      states that have public financing.

      18             The rates of corruption are not lower among

      19      the elected officials with states that have very

      20      harsh campaign finance laws.

      21             And if you look at the states that have

      22      public financing, tax funding, for elections, you

      23      find they're often fraught with new forms of

      24      corruption, leading, in many cases, to new public

      25      cynicism about government, and how effectively and





 

                                                                   14
       1      efficiently it's run.

       2             There's also no evidence that it reduces

       3      special-interest influence in the legislature.

       4             Now, a good part of my testimony, I won't

       5      read it all, because it's 16 pages long, but it

       6      recites many of the forms of corruption we've seen

       7      in New York City from this program.

       8             And I think one way to think of it is:  If

       9      the problem is corrupt politicians, why would you

      10      want to pour gasoline on the fire of corruption by

      11      subsidizing that with tax funds?

      12             If you have people of low moral character,

      13      you don't want to give them more money, and you

      14      certainly don't want to match it at a 6-to-1 rate.

      15             But why stop at 6-to-1?

      16             In the future, I could easily imagine

      17      politicians saying:  We don't have enough money to

      18      compete with interest groups that are running

      19      independent expenditures.  We need a 10-to-1 match,

      20      or a 20-to-1 match.

      21             There's nothing magic about a 6-to-1 match,

      22      from what I can tell.

      23             Some of the problems we have seen in

      24      New York City are:

      25             Phony contributors being named, so they can





 

                                                                   15
       1      get tax financing;

       2             Reimbursed donations, so there can be tax

       3      financing;

       4             And money spent in ways that are not proper

       5      under the New York law.

       6             And I think one thing you should ask yourself

       7      as a committee itself, and perhaps hold hearings on

       8      this:  Has the New York City Council, is it

       9      attracting candidates of higher moral character

      10      today than it was before there was tax financing, or

      11      not?

      12             There should be hearings to find out:

      13             Is there any evidence that the candidates

      14      themselves are of higher moral character?

      15             Are the candidates who are elected, are they

      16      doing a better job?

      17             Is the city council seen as more efficient

      18      and more effective today than it was before

      19      tax-financed elections?

      20             I submit, the answer is "no" to all of those

      21      questions, but you should certainly look into it.

      22             And it's not just New York.

      23             Other states that have tax-financed elections

      24      have had similar problems.  And there are other

      25      problems that will probably emerge that are not even





 

                                                                   16
       1      clear today.

       2             In Arizona, for example, it was clear, some

       3      of the candidates just ran the tax-financed

       4      campaigns as a way of having great parties.

       5             Now, they were eventually run down, and

       6      convicted, but, imagine what the voters thought of

       7      things like that.

       8             You're also likely to see all kinds of gaming

       9      of this type of system, especially when you have a

      10      very lavish match, $6 for every $1 donated.

      11             You're quite likely to see situations, where

      12      one major party thinks, Well, maybe if a minor party

      13      could be propped up, maybe a Green party, or an

      14      extremist right-wing party, it might take votes away

      15      from the Democrats, or the Republicans, as a way of

      16      trying to win a general election.

      17             So you might see operatives of one party or

      18      another trying to get money to these more extreme

      19      parties as a way of trying to tilt the election

      20      field.

      21             So if the worry is corruption, basically, why

      22      would you want to give more state tax funds to

      23      corrupt politicians?

      24             If P.J. O'Rourke was here, he would probably

      25      say, "This is like providing whiskey and car keys to





 

                                                                   17
       1      teenage boys."

       2             You don't want to give corrupt politicians

       3      more and ready sources of funds.

       4             Now, it's often said that these campaign --

       5      tax-financed campaigns are a way of changing

       6      legislative voting patterns.

       7             Our group did an extensive study of the

       8      Connecticut public-financed elections, and we've

       9      compared the voting records of clean-election

      10      participants in the session before the program was

      11      started, and then we looked at it again after it was

      12      over, with the same lawmakers.

      13             And we found, by looking at the five major

      14      interest groups in the state, including the labor

      15      unions, the big business organizations, and such, we

      16      found that the number of times that legislators

      17      voted in favor of the interest groups actually rose

      18      after the clean-election program went into effect,

      19      or, had no impact.

      20             So, that's another question:  If it's being

      21      sold as reducing interest-group impact, there's no

      22      evidence that this has actually happened in

      23      Connecticut.

      24             In fact, it's quite possible, that if you

      25      take a scheme like New York City, interest-group

       1      impact is going to increase, because these groups

       2      have statewide membership lists.  Those members can

       3      be solicited for relatively small-dollar

       4      contributions, where up to a $250 contribution will

      21      goes through.

      22             Supporters of these programs say that

      23      replacing private contributions with taxpayer

      24      dollars will lead to a decrease in the number of

      25      lobbyists and influence of special interests.

       1             We looked at the number of registered

       2      lobbyists before and after these programs.

      16      programs will help root out waste from

      17      special-interest spending.

      18             Well, I would hope that would be true.

      19             We tested this theory by looking at the rate

      20      of growth of government spending in Arizona and

      21      Maine, before and after each state's clean-election

      22      program passed.

      23             And we found that, in fact, state spending in

      24      those states grew at a faster rate than the national

      25      average after the program passed than before.





 

                                                                   20
       1             So, again, there is no impact that we could

       2      see.

       3             Now, I would like to conclude by looking a

       4      little bit at the cost of this program.

       5             I think anyone that can project the cost of

       6      this program.

       7             There's really no way of saying what this

       8      program is going to cost.

       9             You can look at New York City, and that might

      10      be -- might illustrate it, but to take New York City

      11      and to just extrapolate to statewide, I don't think

      12      that's a legitimate way of looking at it.

      13             But even if you did, and you looked at

      14      New York City's costs, you would have to say the

      15      cost would be, per every two-year election cycle,

      16      roughly 160 to 250 million dollars.

      17             But there are a lot of differences between

      18      state elections and city elections.

      19             In New York City, when you win a primary,

      20      you've usually pretty much have won the election.

      21             I mean, there's a general election, but it's

      22      usually a formality.

      23             A lot of the State Assembly and State Senate

      24      races are quite competitive in both the primary and

      25      the general election.

       1             So, you can't just take New York City and

       2      apply it to state elections, districts and

       3      statewide.

       4             And then there's the phenomenon, which is

       5      growing in importance, of independent expenditures.

       6             Independent-expenditure groups are going to

       7      be more active probably in the future, and, how is

       8      that going to influence the cost of elections?

       9             The cost of elections may well go up, and

      10      then there may be a demand in the Legislature to

      13      start at 6-to-1, it could be 10-to-1 in the future,

      15             I don't know what a future legislature might

      16      adopt.

      17             So, I think it's possible you could see the

      18      program ballooning cost far beyond even what are

      19      seen as high projections today, into the future.

      20             It could be a quarter billion.  It could be a

      21      half billion.  It could even be more.

      22             There's really no way of knowing.

      23             And, with the combination of statewide

      24      interest groups that are able to raise money at a

      25      6-to-1 match, working with the candidates, we could

       1      see explosive costs in campaigns.  There's really no

       2      way of knowing.

       3             And then there's another thing I hope you'll

       4      reflect on:

       5             There are often extreme parties that come

       6      along.

       7             I mean, you -- I don't know who hasn't run

      17      organizations, propagating these extreme views that

      18      I totally disagree with?

       1      you'll see, in almost every case, there's no change,

       2      corruption doesn't go down, these other effects

       6             And I would leave you with the thought of
